This play is also remarkable because one team had stolen a point from another earlier in the season on a bad goal reversal call. With the trailing team down by one with less than a minute to go, a player took the draw in the offensive zone. He won the faceoff and assisted on a tying goal, but the whole play was redone because the referee thought that the player had made a hand pass when in fact his hand was just low on his stick for the faceoff. The trailing team failed to recreate their quick goal, the leading team won in regulation, and I had no problem with the result at the time, though I acknowledged that it was a raw deal for the trailing team. This play has everything: a player scores, a commentator criticizes a bad performance, a whole team gets screwed. I didn't think much of it until this happened, weeks or months later. This sense of failure can stem from various factors, including personal challenges, societal pressures, or unmet expectations. Moreover, the fear of judgment from peers can prevent individuals from seeking help or expressing their struggles, leading to isolation. It's essential to recognize that everyone faces challenges and that failure is a part of the human experience. Embracing vulnerability and seeking support can be crucial steps toward overcoming these feelings and finding a path to personal fulfillment. 

Ultimately, redefining what success means on an individual level can help alleviate the pressure to conform to societal standards, allowing for a more authentic and satisfying life journey.

I don't necessarily mean simply who signs the cheques or who receives the immediate product of your work, but rather to spur thinking about what the actual concept of work means to a given person, if there are different opportunities to serve someone else's needs, and maybe lead to outcomes such as better understanding of people's motivations or what would constitute a satisfying career for an individual. Pro tip: beans in a baked potato is an excellent combo because it covers protein, carbs, and fiber without too much fat. It's worth noting that the skin of the potato contains much of its nutrients and fiber. In fact, let me talk for a second about the role of fiber in a healthy diet.

When ingested with carbs, (e.g. rice or potatoes), fiber slows down the digestion of said carbs, allowing them to enter your bloodstream as glucose more gradually than if you just ate the carbs on their own. This is the difference between a sugar rush and a good meal that keeps you energized for longer. The short-term effect of eating carbs without fiber is an energy spike followed by a crash, and the long-term effect is often weight gain. For more on this concept, do some cursory research on the glycemic index, also sometimes known as "fast vs slow carbs." For people eating on a budget, it can be easy and tempting to just live off of white rice and call it good, but a little better understanding of how the body converts food to energy can go a long way toward a healthy life.
